name: Intervention Studies
text: Intervention studies Ass.Prof: Dr Heba El Weshahy 1 EBM Differentiate between observational and intervention studies Draw the flow chart of randomized controlled trial Explain the main characteristics of intervention studies Identify different designs of conducting RCT State advantages and limitations of of RCT Intended learning outcomes: By the end of this lecture you will be able to : Primary research Observational Intervention (Experimental) In which one observes the course of a disease Are used to address questions about prevalence, natural history, etiology, and risk groups. In which one intervenes to prevent or change the course of a disease, Are used to evaluate preventive or therapeutic interventions, The investigator passively observes as nature takes its course The investigators actively manipulate the exposure (has a control) Intervention (Experimental) studies Each time a vaccine, drug, medical device or procedure, is tested, an experiment (a research) is conducted, results are analyzed, and a conclusion is reached. The main question in these experiments “Is this intervention effective and safe? 4 The main purpose of intervention study Effectiveness: Is the ability to produce the desired results Safety: Freedom from danger, side effects, risks, threats of harm or injury. Intervention (Experimental) studies An intervention study is a follow-up study in which the intervention (proposed exposure) under study is applied by the investigator (researcher) to individuals or a community. Phases of clinical trials : Randomized controlled clinical trial Participants Randomly Assigned Follow - Up Follow - Up Outcome Compared Intervention Group Control Group Intervention Group Control Group Randomized controlled clinical trial Participants Are allocated at random Into 2 or more groups (one of them is control)To receive one or more interventions, then Followed up in time, and outcomes are compared Examples of outcomes (End points) Recurrence Mortality Disease incidence Recovery rate(cure) Symptom releif Quality of life Principles of RCT Randomization Presence of control group Blinding (masking) 1. Randomization Each member of the sample included in the study has the same probability of allocation to the treatment or the control arm It could be done by using computer programs or other methods of randomization 2. The Control Arm How: Criteria for inclusion (Eligibility criteria) Examples of control arm: Standard Care/treatment Placebo Careful follow up (no intervention) Higher or lower dose 14 A placebo is a treatment that looks the same as the potential new medicine but has no active ingredients 14 3. Blinding: “Hiding who gets what” Masking the identity of the assigned interventions Main goal: avoid potential bias caused by conscious or subconscious factors Single blinding: patients are blinded Double blinding: both patients and investigators are blinded Triple blinding: blinding of patients, investigators, and statisticians Sometimes blinding is impossible. E.g. it may be difficult to blind the physician in a surgery 15 15 RCT Designs RCT Designs Parallel design Each group is subjected to one intervention (the most common design) 17 17 RCT Designs Factorial Design: A secondary treatment administered concurrently with the primary treatment to permit examination of the modification of the main and interactive effects of each. (Does The effect of treatment A differs depending upon the presence or absence of intervention B and vice-versa) 18 Group 1: Aspirin (to prevent cardiovascular disease) and beta carotene placebo Group 2: Beta-carotene (to prevent cancer) and aspirin placebo Group 3: Aspirin and beta-carotene Group 4: Beta carotene placebo and aspirin placebo Subjects are randomized to sequences of treatments (A then B or B then A) Uses the patient as his/her own control Often a “wash-out” period (time between treatment periods) is used to avoid a “carry over” effect (the effect of treatment in the first period affecting outcomes in the second period) Can have a cross-over design with more than 2 periods 18 RCT Designs Cross – Over design Each participant is given both interventions in successive periods. Each participant acts as his or her own control. 19 Subjects are randomized to sequences of treatments (A then B or B then A) Uses the patient as his/her own control Often a “wash-out” period (time between treatment periods) is used to avoid a “carry over” effect (the effect of treatment in the first period affecting outcomes in the second period) Can have a cross-over design with more than 2 periods 19 Advantages of RCTs Best method for evaluating effectiveness of an intervention Randomization avoids selection and confounding biases Blinding can avoid information bias Explaining cause and effect relationship Disadvantages of RCTs: Difficult, time consuming and expensive. Late outcomes require long period of follow up may lead to attrition bias Multiple Ethical issues …… Not possible to use RCT’s to test effects of exposures that are expected to be harmful (e.g pregnancy outcomes and alcohol consumption) Thank you
